screens.body: Real programs make decisions. If it's raining, take an umbrella; otherwise, don't. Code works the same way: if a condition is true, do this; otherwise, do that. Conditionals bend the flow of control — instead of running every line top to bottom, the program chooses its path.

options: Choose what to do based on a condition
check.question: Conditionals let a program…

screens.heading: Programs make decisions

screens.body: The if statement runs its block only when the condition is true. Add an else, and you cover the 'otherwise' case. The condition sits in parentheses; the code to run sits in braces. Only one branch ever runs — if the condition is true, the else is skipped entirely.

check.question: If age is 16, what prints here?

screens.heading: if and else
screens.keyPoint: if runs when true; else covers everything else.

screens.body: Conditions ask yes-or-no questions with comparison operators: == (equal), != (not equal), > < >= <=. You can combine them: && means AND (both must be true), || means OR (at least one), ! means NOT (flips it). Read them out loud — 'age >= 18 && hasTicket' literally means 'age is 18 or more AND has a ticket.'

options: 18 or older AND has a ticket
check.question: age >= 18 && hasTicket means…

screens.heading: Comparing and combining

screens.body: When there are more than two paths, chain them with else if. Java checks each condition top to bottom and runs the FIRST one that's true — then skips the rest. Order matters: put the most specific condition first, or a broader one above it will steal the match.
screens.heading: else if chains
screens.keyPoint: First true branch wins; order matters.

screens.body: When you're choosing between many values of ONE variable, switch is cleaner than a long else-if chain. Each case is one possible value, and break stops Java from falling through into the next case. Forget break, and every case below the match runs too — the classic switch bug.
screens.heading: switch: many options, one value
screens.keyPoint: switch picks one value; break stops the fall-through.

screens.body: Conditions can live inside other conditions — that's nesting. The inner if only gets checked when the outer one is true. Nesting is powerful but keep it shallow: more than two levels deep gets hard to read. When it gets tangled, && can often flatten it into one condition.

They run at the same time

screens.heading: Nesting: if inside if
screens.keyPoint: Inner conditions only run when outer ones pass.

screens.body: The most classic beginner bug: = assigns, == compares. Writing if (ready = false) doesn't check anything — it SETS ready to false, and the block never runs. Java won't always warn you. Inside an if, you almost always want == (or === in JavaScript). Read your conditions twice.

screens.heading: The classic mistake: = vs ==
screens.keyPoint: = assigns; == compares. Don't mix them up.
